new_statements.quote: Stress in Paiwan generally falls on the penultimate syllable (Ho 1977; Ferrell 1982; Egli 1990). Stress is on the ultima under three circumstances in most communalects: (i) when the final syllable of a prosodic word is derived from underlying vowel hiatus, (ii) when the word is monosyllabic, and (iii) when a prefix/infix is adhered to a monosyllabic root. … The default penultimate stress is on the final syllable only when the ultima is a heavy syllable, the word is monosyllabic, or when the penult is a prefix/infix. These patterns, including the shifting of stress to heavy syllables formed from underlying hiatus, hold true for all Paiwan communalects.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2) records plain penultimate stress. Yeh 2017 agrees that penultimate is the default and pervasive pattern for Paiwan as a whole, and refines it: (1) a heavy (bimoraic, hiatus-derived) ultima attracts stress in all communalects, which is compatible with the catalog if vowel sequences are counted heterosyllabically as Ho 1977 does (then stress is still on the penultimate vowel); (2) monosyllables and affix+monosyllabic-root words are final-stressed; (3) in the central communalects (Piuma, Kazangiljan, Qapedang, Kazazaljan, Ulaljuc, Kaviyangan and some Taitung villages) stress is weight/schwa-sensitive within the final two syllables, which is a variety-specific departure…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is always on one of the last two syllables. For Paiwan in general the default is the penultimate syllable; it falls on the ultima only when the ultima is heavy (a diphthong or coalesced vowel derived from underlying vowel hiatus, e.g. /sikau/ [si.káw], /pu-vasa-an/ [pu.va.sán]), when the word is monosyllabic, or when the penult is a prefix/infix on a monosyllabic root (affixes cannot bear stress; suffixes -u/-i/-an do not attract stress). In the central communalects the paper focuses on (Piuma, Kazangiljan and neighbours) stress additionally avoids schwa: penult schwa + final full vowel gives final stress ([kə.rí] 'small', [qa.pə.dú] 'gall'); if both of the last two vowels are schwa, stress goes to the ultima when it is closed ([ʧə.kə́ʎ] 'spouse') and otherwise reverts to the penult ([vǝ́.vǝ] 'to sprout'). Yeh analyses this as quantity-sensitivity with coerced coda weight (vs. Chen 2009 / Yeh 2011a quality-sensitive accounts).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: '"In Paiwan, the location of stress is confined to the rightmost two syllables of a prosodic word, and penultimate stress is the overwhelming pattern seen in the data above. No secondary stress is observed."' (p. 552, §6). A single right-aligned trochaic foot is assumed.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Final stress on a heavy ultima derived from vowel hiatus (glide formation or coalescence), in all communalects; (b) monosyllables and prefix/infix + monosyllabic root take final stress ([kǝ.mán] 'eat (AV)', [pa.kán] 'to feed'); (c) central-communalect schwa avoidance: p. 547 'To summarize the data from the central communalects, penultimate stress is prevalent when no schwa is present in the rightmost two-syllable domain. Furthermore, stress avoids falling on schwa /ə/ within the domain unless the last two vowels are both schwa. Under these conditions, stress is assigned to the ultima if it is a closed syllable; otherwise, stress is placed on the penultima by default.' (d) Other communalects such as Sinvaudjan keep penultimate stress regardless of vowel quality ([kə́.ɖi], [qa.pə́.du]); fn. 8 reports Cheng (2016, 131-132) that in Puljetji village stress is always penultimate regardless of morphological structure (even on a prefix/infix). Medial nasal codas from schwa deletion give surface final stress in central villages ([vaŋ.sáʀ] vs Sinvaudjan [váŋ.saʀ]).
new_statements.identity_note: Yeh 2017 describes the stress of a subset of central Paiwan villages (Piuma and Kazangiljan explicitly; also Qapedang, Kazazaljan, Ulaljuc, Kaviyangan, and some Taitung County villages founded from them), contrasted with 'most Paiwan communalects' exemplified by Sinvaudjan; fn. 8 also cites Cheng 2016 on Puljetji. The author uses 'communalect' rather than 'dialect' (fn. 1). The general-Paiwan statements (pp. 543-544) are explicitly said to hold for all communalects. Directory also already held Chen 2004, Chen 2009 and Shih 2018 from an earlier reading; they were not in this task's works list and were not re-read.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction with the catalog for Paiwan in general: Yeh 2017 states that penultimate stress is the pervasive pattern and that most communalects (e.g. Sinvaudjan, and Puljetji per Cheng 2016) stress the penult regardless of vowel quality. The disagreement is internal to the language: the central communalects (Piuma, Kazangiljan and neighbours) avoid stressing schwa and show weight-sensitive stress within the last two syllables, which Yeh analyses as quantity-sensitivity (peripheral vowels heavier than schwa, coerced coda weight) against the quality-/sonority-sensitive analyses of Chen 2009 and Yeh 2011a. The hiatus-derived heavy-ultima exception (all communalects) is analysis-dependent: Ferrell 1982 and Ho 1977 treat vowel sequences as heterosyllabic, under which those words are simply penultimate by vowel count; Egli 1990, Chen 2006/2009 and Yeh treat them as tautosyllabic diphthongs, under which the ultima is heavy and stressed.

sources.quote: 'Paiwan stress falls on penultimate syllables in general. However, there are a few exceptions. (7) a. In CV or CVCV syllables, stress falls on the first V; b. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable elsewhere; c. Stress patterns are fixed in content words but not fixed in function words, reduplicated and affixed forms; d. If the nucleus of the penultimate syllable is a weak schwa, stress shifts to the last syllable' (Piuma Paiwan; acoustic correlates duration/pitch/intensity tested in 5.2).
